questions.question: What is Amazon S3 and what type of storage does it provide?
questions.answer: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's scalable, durable object storage service. It stores data as objects — each consisting of the data content, a unique key (name), and metadata. Unlike EBS (block storage) or EFS (file storage), S3 is accessed via HTTP/HTTPS API, not mounted as a disk. It can store any amount of data and serve it globally.

questions.question: What is the difference between an S3 bucket and an S3 object?
questions.answer: A bucket is a container for objects — like a folder at the top level. You create the bucket first, then store objects inside it. An object is any file or data stored in S3, consisting of the data itself, a unique key (full path/name within the bucket), and metadata. Buckets have globally unique names; objects have keys unique within their bucket.

questions.question: Why must S3 bucket names be globally unique?
questions.answer: Every S3 bucket automatically gets a DNS name in the format bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com. Since DNS requires globally unique hostnames, two buckets cannot share the same name — just like domain names on the internet. This uniqueness spans all AWS accounts and all regions worldwide.

questions.question: What is S3's durability guarantee for the Standard storage class?
questions.answer: S3 Standard provides 99.999999999% durability — eleven nines. This means if you store 10 million objects, you can expect to lose at most one per 10,000 years. It is achieved by automatically storing data across a minimum of 3 Availability Zones within a region. Note: this protects against hardware failures and AZ outages, but NOT against accidental deletion.

questions.question: What is S3's flat namespace and why does it matter?
questions.answer: S3 does not have a real directory structure. Object keys are just strings — when a key contains '/' characters like 'reports/2024/q4.pdf', S3 treats this as a single key name. The console displays '/' separators as visual folders for convenience, but no actual directories exist. This matters for listing operations, prefix searches, and performance optimization.

questions.question: What are S3 storage classes and when would you use each?
questions.answer: S3 storage classes balance cost vs access speed: Standard (frequent access, highest cost, 11 nines, multi-AZ), Standard-IA (monthly access, retrieval fee, 30-day minimum), One Zone-IA (single AZ, cheap, data loss risk), Intelligent-Tiering (auto-moves between tiers based on access), Glacier Instant Retrieval (quarterly access, ms retrieval), Glacier Flexible Retrieval (backup archives, 1-12 hr retrieval), Glacier Deep Archive (7+ year compliance, 12-48 hr retrieval, cheapest). Match the class to how frequently you access the data.

questions.question: What is S3 Versioning and how does it protect against accidental deletion?
questions.answer: Versioning preserves all versions of every object. When enabled: overwriting a file creates a new version (old version preserved); deleting a file creates a delete marker (object hidden but versions preserved). You can restore any previous version at any time. To permanently delete, you must explicitly delete individual version IDs. Versioning is the first line of defense against accidental data loss in S3.

questions.question: What is the maximum size of an S3 object and when is Multipart Upload required?
questions.answer: A single S3 object can be up to 5 TB. Multipart Upload is required for objects larger than 5 GB — this API splits the upload into parts (up to 10,000 parts), uploads them in parallel, then assembles them. AWS recommends using Multipart Upload for objects larger than 100 MB because it's faster (parallel upload) and recoverable (resume failed parts without restarting the entire upload).

questions.question: How is S3 a 'global service' and what does that mean for data storage?
questions.answer: S3 has a single global dashboard — all buckets from all regions appear in one view regardless of which region the console is set to. This is unlike EC2, which shows per-region resources. However, each bucket's data physically resides in the specific region where the bucket was created. Data does NOT auto-replicate across regions — you need Cross-Region Replication (CRR) for that.

questions.question: What is the default access setting for an S3 bucket and how do you make objects public?
questions.answer: By default, all S3 buckets and objects are private, with Block Public Access enabled. Only the bucket owner can access them. To make objects publicly accessible: 1) Disable Block Public Access settings, 2) Add a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject to Principal: '*', 3) OR set individual object ACLs to public-read. Public access should only be used intentionally for specific use cases like static website hosting.

questions.question: A startup's S3 storage costs are $3,000/month. An analysis shows 70% of objects haven't been accessed in 45 days. How would you reduce cost?
questions.answer: (Situation) High S3 costs, mostly inactive data. (Task) Reduce cost with minimal effort. (Action) Created S3 Lifecycle policies: transition objects to Standard-IA after 30 days (70% of data at ~80% cost reduction for storage). For objects older than 90 days and not accessed, transition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval (additional savings). Enabled S3 Storage Class Analysis to validate access patterns before committing. (Result) Projected cost dropped from $3,000 to under $700/month — ~77% savings — with no application changes and no data loss.

questions.question: Users upload images to S3. Some users report their uploads fail for large files. How do you diagnose and fix?
questions.answer: (Situation) Large file uploads failing. (Task) Identify threshold and fix. (Action) Checked the application SDK version and upload method — found it was using a single PUT request. Objects over 5 GB fail with a single PUT. Implemented Multipart Upload in the application: files under 100MB use single PUT; files 100MB+ automatically use Multipart Upload via the S3 SDK's managed upload feature. Also set the S3 bucket lifecycle policy to abort incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days to prevent storage of orphaned parts. (Result) All uploads now succeed regardless of size.

questions.question: A hacker gained temporary access to AWS and deleted all objects in your critical S3 bucket. How do you recover?
questions.answer: (Situation) All objects in S3 bucket deleted by unauthorized access. (Task) Recover data. (Action) If versioning was enabled: the deletes created delete markers. Recovery: used AWS CLI to list all delete markers, deleted the delete markers — this restored all objects to their previous state. If versioning was NOT enabled: objects are permanently gone unless AWS Backup was in place. Lesson applied: immediately enabled versioning on all buckets, enabled MFA Delete for additional protection, added S3 Object Lock for critical buckets. (Result) Data recovered within 30 minutes via delete marker removal.

questions.question: Your company needs to host a static website (HTML, CSS, JS, images) accessible worldwide with the lowest possible latency. Design the solution.
questions.answer: (Situation) Static website, global users, low latency required. (Task) Design cost-effective global delivery. (Action) Stored all static assets in an S3 bucket with Static Website Hosting enabled. Disabled Block Public Access and applied a bucket policy for s3:GetObject. Created an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as origin. Enabled CloudFront caching at 300+ edge locations worldwide. Used Route 53 to point domain to the CloudFront distribution. (Result) Users served from nearest edge location — sub-50ms load times globally. S3 origin gets only cache-miss requests. Cost-effective at scale with virtually unlimited traffic capacity.

questions.question: You need to give a third-party vendor read-only access to a specific folder in your S3 bucket without giving them AWS credentials. How do you do this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Third-party needs access to specific S3 path, no credentials sharing. (Task) Grant least-privilege access securely. (Action) Created a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket with a condition restricting the prefix to the specific 'folder' (key prefix). Created an IAM role in the account the vendor will assume via cross-account access (if they have an AWS account) OR generated a pre-signed URL for specific objects with a time-limited expiry for one-time access. For ongoing access without credentials: used S3 Access Points — created one with a policy scoped to the specific prefix. (Result) Vendor has scoped access; main bucket policy and other prefixes are untouched.

questions.question: What are S3 pre-signed URLs and when would you use them?
questions.answer: A pre-signed URL is a time-limited, pre-authenticated URL that grants temporary access to a specific S3 object without requiring AWS credentials. Generated by an IAM identity with access to the object, the URL encodes the credentials and expiry time. Use cases: allowing a user to download a private file for 1 hour; allowing a user to upload directly to S3 without routing through your server; temporary sharing of confidential documents. Expiry can be from seconds to 7 days (7-day max with permanent IAM credentials; 1-hour max with temporary STS credentials).

questions.question: What is S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) and what are its requirements?
questions.answer: CRR automatically replicates objects from a source bucket to a destination bucket in a different AWS region. Requirements: 1) Versioning must be enabled on BOTH source and destination buckets; 2) An IAM role with S3 replication permissions must be configured; 3) The destination bucket can be in the same or a different AWS account. CRR replicates all new objects (existing objects must be replicated using S3 Batch Replication). Use cases: disaster recovery across regions, data sovereignty compliance, latency reduction for global users.

questions.question: A compliance team requires that certain S3 objects cannot be deleted for 5 years — not even by admins. What feature do you use?
questions.answer: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode. When an object is locked in Compliance mode: it cannot be deleted or overwritten by any user — including the root AWS account — until the retention period expires. The retention period cannot be shortened once set. This satisfies regulatory requirements like SEC 17a-4, FINRA, and HIPAA that require tamper-proof immutable records. Configure: enable Object Lock at bucket creation, apply Compliance mode retention (5 years = 1825 days) to the objects or via a default bucket-level policy.

questions.question: What is S3 Transfer Acceleration and when does it provide benefit?
questions.answer: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest AWS CloudFront edge location, then transfers the data to the destination S3 bucket via AWS's private backbone network instead of the public internet. This benefits uploads from geographically distant locations — a user in Australia uploading to a bucket in us-east-1 will see significant speed improvement. For same-region or nearby uploads, Transfer Acceleration provides little benefit and adds cost. AWS provides a comparison tool to test whether acceleration actually helps for your specific scenario.

questions.question: How does S3 Lifecycle policy work and what transitions are allowed?
questions.answer: S3 Lifecycle policies automate moving objects between storage classes and expiring them. Transitions follow a waterfall — objects can only move to lower-cost (less available) classes, never back up. Allowed transitions: Standard → Standard-IA (after 30-day minimum), Standard-IA → Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Instant → Glacier Flexible, Glacier Flexible → Glacier Deep Archive. Expiration actions delete objects or versions after a specified age. Each storage class has a minimum storage duration — moving objects before this duration incurs the minimum charge regardless.

questions.question: Design a complete S3 architecture for a healthcare application that needs to store patient medical images with 10-year retention, HIPAA compliance, and disaster recovery.
questions.answer: Architecture: Two S3 buckets — primary (ap-south-1) and DR replica (us-east-1). Enable versioning on both. Enable S3 Object Lock (Compliance mode, 10-year retention) on both. Enable SSE-KMS encryption with a customer-managed KMS key (CMK). Enable Cross-Region Replication from primary to DR with S3 Replication Time Control (15-minute SLA). Configure lifecycle: Standard → Glacier Instant Retrieval after 90 days → Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year. Enable S3 server access logging and CloudTrail for all S3 API calls (HIPAA audit requirement). Configure bucket policy denying s3:DeleteObject (belt-and-suspenders with Object Lock). Enable S3 Inventory for periodic compliance reporting. Result: HIPAA-compliant, encrypted, immutable, geo-redundant storage with tiered cost optimization.

questions.question: What is S3 Intelligent-Tiering and how does it differ from using manual Lifecycle policies?
questions.answer: Intelligent-Tiering monitors each object's access patterns and moves it between tiers automatically without any retrieval fees. Tiers: Frequent Access (Standard equivalent), Infrequent Access (Standard-IA equivalent, after 30 days no access), Archive Instant Access (Glacier Instant equivalent, after 90 days), optional Archive and Deep Archive tiers. Differences from Lifecycle policies: Lifecycle is time-based (move after N days regardless of access); Intelligent-Tiering is access-pattern-based (move only when not accessed). Lifecycle is predictable and has no monitoring fee; Intelligent-Tiering charges a small monthly monitoring fee per object but no retrieval fees. Choose Intelligent-Tiering for unpredictable or varying access patterns; Lifecycle for well-understood, time-based patterns.

questions.question: How would you optimize S3 read performance for an application with high request rates (10,000+ requests/second)?
questions.answer: S3 can handle 3,500 PUT/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix. To scale beyond this: 1) Use multiple key prefixes — distribute objects across different prefixes (e.g., hash-prefix the key) to parallelize across partitions; 2) Add Amazon CloudFront as a CDN to cache frequently read objects at edge locations — reduces S3 origin load; 3) Use S3 byte-range fetches for large objects — read in parallel; 4) Enable S3 Request Metrics in CloudWatch to monitor actual request rates; 5) Use S3 Batch Operations for bulk operations instead of individual API calls. For read-heavy static content, CloudFront alone often reduces S3 GET requests by 90%+.

questions.question: What is the difference between S3 Server-Side Encryption modes: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, and SSE-C?
questions.answer: SSE-S3: AWS manages the encryption keys entirely. AES-256 encryption. Default since January 2023. No extra cost. You cannot audit key usage. SSE-KMS: Encryption keys are managed in AWS KMS. You control the key policy, can rotate the key, and get full CloudTrail audit logs of every decrypt operation. Small cost per API call. Required for environments needing key usage auditability (HIPAA, PCI-DSS). SSE-C: You provide the encryption key with every request. AWS uses it to encrypt/decrypt but never stores the key. Maximum control — but you are responsible for secure key management. If you lose the key, data is permanently inaccessible. Choose SSE-KMS for regulated environments needing audit trails; SSE-C for maximum key control with your own key management infrastructure.

questions.question: What is S3 Object Lambda and when would you use it?
questions.answer: S3 Object Lambda allows you to add custom code (Lambda functions) to process S3 objects on-the-fly as they are retrieved. Instead of retrieving the raw object, the data passes through your Lambda function before being returned to the caller. Use cases: automatically redact PII (personally identifiable information) from documents before serving; resize images on-the-fly based on the requesting client; convert file formats (CSV to JSON) at retrieval time; watermark images. This eliminates the need to maintain derivative copies of the same data in different formats — you store one copy and transform at retrieval. Requires S3 Access Point and Object Lambda Access Point configuration.
